unit.title: Food chains and food webs
unit.blurb: How energy passes from plants to animals, how food chains join into webs, and how people can harm or protect them.

O1.t: Describe producers and consumers, draw food chains with arrows that show the flow of energy, and use the words predator, prey and herbivore.

O2.t: Read food webs and predict what happens when one population changes.

O3.t: Explain why only a little energy is passed along each step of a food chain.

O4.t: Describe how toxic substances, such as pesticides and metals, accumulate along food chains.

O5.t: Describe how microplastics, pollution and habitat loss harm food webs, and how people can protect them.

captions: Hello, nature scientists!
This is lesson 4.1: food chains, food webs and energy.
All living things need energy to live and grow.
Green plants make their own food, using energy from sunlight.
Because plants produce food, we call them producers.
Animals cannot make their own food. They eat plants or other animals. They are consumers.
A food chain shows what eats what.
Grass is eaten by a rabbit, and the rabbit is eaten by a fox.
The arrows point in the direction the food and energy move: from the grass, to the rabbit, to the fox.
Pause and think. In a food chain, which way do the arrows point?
A food chain always starts with a producer, a green plant.
An animal that eats only plants is a herbivore.
An animal that hunts and eats other animals is a predator. The animal it eats is its prey.
Most animals eat more than one kind of food, and are eaten by more than one kind of animal.
So food chains join together to make a food web.
Here, the grasshopper and the rabbit both eat grass, and the fox and the owl both hunt the mouse.
Your turn. Look at the food web. Which animal eats more than one kind of food?
Energy passes along the food chain, from one living thing to the next.
But at each step, most of the energy is used for moving, growing and keeping warm.
Only a little is passed on. That is why there are many plants, fewer rabbits, and even fewer foxes.
If one population changes, the whole web can change.
Imagine the rabbits catch a disease and many die.
The foxes have less food, so their numbers may fall.
But the grass has fewer animals eating it, so it may grow more.
Let's remember.
Plants are producers, and animals are consumers.
The arrows show the direction the food and energy move.
Food chains join together into food webs.
And only a little energy is passed on at each step.
Great work! Now go to the practice room and say the new words.

captions: Welcome back, nature scientists!
This is lesson 4.2: harm to food chains and food webs.
Farmers sometimes spray crops with pesticides, to kill insects that eat the crops.
But pesticides can be toxic. That means poisonous.
Rain can wash them into rivers and lakes, where other living things take them in.
Tiny water plants take in a little of the pesticide.
Small fish eat lots of these plants, so the poison builds up in their bodies.
A big bird eats lots of small fish, so it gets the most poison of all.
We say the toxic substance accumulates along the food chain.
Pause and think. Which animal gets the most poison, the small fish or the big bird?
Plastic rubbish in the sea breaks into very small pieces, called microplastics.
Tiny sea animals eat them by mistake. Then fish eat those animals.
The plastic passes along the ocean food chain, and it can end up in the fish that people eat.
Other things harm food webs too.
Factories can let toxic metals, like mercury, into rivers.
Cutting down forests and oil spills destroy the homes and food of many living things.
Your turn. What are microplastics?
We can all help to protect food webs.
Use less plastic, and reuse and recycle it.
Never drop litter, especially near water.
Farmers can use natural pest control, like ladybirds that eat aphids.
And we can plant trees and wild flowers for animals to live in.
Let's remember.
Pesticides and some metals are toxic.
Toxic substances build up, or accumulate, along food chains.
Microplastics pass along ocean food chains.
And we can help by using less plastic and protecting habitats.
Fantastic work! See you in the practice room.
